title: Early Clinical and Inflammatory Predictors of Severe Acute Lower Respiratory Infection in Hospitalized Children: A Multivariable Analysis
content: Early identification of children at risk of severe acute respiratory infection remains a clinical challenge. Although C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and white blood cell (WBC) count are commonly assessed at hospital admission, their predictive value in severity assessment remains uncertain. We aimed to evaluate the utility of clinical features, respiratory multiplex PCR test detecting 23 pathogens, imaging findings, and early inflammatory biomarkers in predicting severe acute respiratory tract infection (ALRI) among hospitalized children. The primary outcome was the requirement for supplemental oxygen during hospitalization, used as a marker of severe disease. We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study including children admitted to the pediatric department between May 2022 and June 2023 with ALRI or other conditions in which respiratory infection was considered and subsequently excluded. All included patients underwent multiplex respiratory PCR testing. We included 439 children in the analysis [median age, 20 mo (IQR: 5–54); 52.7% males]. Out of them 178 (40.5%) had severe ALRI. The strongest positive associations with severity were shown for low oxygen saturation on admission [OR 8.83 (95% CI, 3.00–26.02; p < 0.001)]. The strongest predictors of severe disease in multivariable analysis were age, abnormal auscultatory findings, and the number of danger signs. For the prediction of severe pediatric pneumonia, no single marker offered robust utility. These findings may support clinical decision-making during triage and hospitalization in identifying children who may benefit from closer monitoring and targeted interventions.
